tldr: By fast-computing tangential contact motion as "simulated tactile flow" directly in a rigid-body simulator and translating real tactile image streams into this flow alongside contact depth, the authors achieve high-performance sim-to-real tactile manipulation without relying on computationally expensive soft-body physics.
hero_caption: Overview of the TactileLab framework. Built on IsaacLab, it efficiently computes "tactile flow" via GPU-parallel rigid-body simulation. Policies trained with PETS-Net are transferred zero-shot to real-world hardware—demonstrated on dual-arm following and dexterous in-hand rotation—via real-to-sim translation of real tactile images.
overview:
When a robot dextrously manipulates objects with its fingertips, shear information—slip, twisting, and tangential displacement between object and sensor—is critically important. However, existing tactile simulators face a dilemma. Soft-body simulators that faithfully model elastomer deformation are too slow for large-scale reinforcement learning (RL). Conversely, fast rigid-body simulators typically only output normal contact depth (penetration), completely ignoring shear.

To resolve this trade-off, the authors introduce "simulated tactile flow," an optical-flow-like representation of dense tangential motion at the contact interface computed purely within rigid-body simulation. This makes it possible to generate rich, paired high-dimensional tactile observations—contact depth (geometry) and tactile flow (tangential motion)—at high throughput without finite element methods (FEM).

To bridge the sim-to-real gap, they also developed "TacFlowNet," an image translation model that predicts simulated tactile flow from consecutive real tactile camera frames. They validated it across diverse vision-based tactile sensors, including TacTip, GelSight Mini, and 9DTact.

In experiments spanning dual-arm contact following and continuous in-hand object rotation using a 16-DoF multi-fingered hand (LEAP Hand), policies incorporating tactile flow significantly outperformed prior baselines. Remarkably, despite being trained solely on simple capsules in simulation, the real-world policy continuously rotated previously unseen everyday objects, such as sharp cubes and fruits, without dropping them.
contributions: Formulated "simulated tactile flow," which efficiently derives dense tangential motion fields from rigid-body contact geometry and kinematics without soft-body physics.
Built "TactileLab" on top of IsaacLab, a scalable multimodal tactile simulator compatible with GPU-parallel reinforcement learning.

Designed "PETS-Net," a policy architecture that efficiently fuses long-horizon proprioceptive and action histories with high-dimensional tactile observations using positional encoding and spatio-temporal networks.
Developed "TacFlowNet," a pix2pix-based real-to-sim translation network that predicts simulated tactile flow from real tactile image streams across heterogeneous sensors.
Demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for dual-arm tracking and multi-fingered in-hand manipulation, showing remarkable generalization to unseen object geometries.

sections.heading: Why is shear vital for touch, and why has simulating it been so hard?
sections.summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires perceiving shear and slip, but soft-body simulation is too slow, and rigid-body simulation typically only models normal penetration depth. TactileLab resolves this dilemma by calculating dense tangential motion vectors directly from rigid-body physics as "simulated tactile flow."
sections.details:
For robots to manipulate objects delicately, they must quickly detect subtle force changes and early signs of slip at the fingertips. Vision-based tactile sensors are attractive because they provide high-resolution observations. However, replicating them in simulation for large-scale reinforcement learning poses a major hurdle.

Existing tactile simulators generally fall into two categories. Soft-body simulators, often using finite element methods (FEM), accurately capture elastomer deformation, but their heavy computational footprint makes them unsuitable for parallel RL requiring millions or billions of steps. On the other hand, rigid-body simulators run very fast, but most of them only render penetration depth (contact depth) into the sensor surface. Normal depth alone cannot reveal which direction an object is slipping or twisting. As a result, identical depth images can correspond to completely different contact dynamics, creating severe partial observability that hinders policy learning.

This is where TactileLab steps in. The authors bypass expensive soft-body physics by calculating relative tangential motion at the contact interface as a 2D vector field—termed "simulated tactile flow"—directly from rigid-body simulation. This enables a fast, high-dimensional tactile platform that provides both normal contact geometry (depth map) and tangential motion (tactile flow).

sections.heading: The landscape of tactile simulation and sim-to-real transfer
sections.summary: Prior rigid-body simulators lacked shear representations, and recent shear-aware methods required precomputed signed distance functions (SDFs). Furthermore, sim-to-real for dexterous hands has largely relied on proprioception or low-dimensional contact points, leaving dense temporal tactile flow unexplored.
sections.details:
### II-A Evolution of Tactile Simulation
Existing tactile simulators are broadly split into rigid-body (Tactile Gym, TACTO) and soft-body approaches. Rigid simulators generate contacts quickly from penetration depth, but they focus on instantaneous normal contact and neglect shear. Soft-body simulators track marker displacement or mesh deformation, providing high fidelity at throughputs far too low for massively parallel RL. Recent approaches like TacSL and HydroShear approximate shear forces on rigid bodies, but they require precomputed Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) of the objects, limiting their general applicability. TactileLab differs fundamentally because it derives dense flow fields directly from rigid-body kinematics without requiring object SDFs.

### II-B Sim-to-Real Tactile Policies
For robot arms, image translation methods paired with simulation depth (such as the Tactile Gym series) have become well-established. In contrast, dexterous manipulation has largely relied on estimating latent state from joint-angle history (HORA), binary touch feedback (Touch Dexterity), or low-dimensional contact positions and normal forces (AnyRotate). Using dense, temporal tactile representations across heterogeneous sensors and distinct robot embodiments remained largely unexplored.

captions.F2: The simulation pipeline and tactile flow computation in TactileLab. Contact patches from rigid-body simulation are projected onto the tactile camera's image plane, and per-pixel displacement vectors are computed from relative motion between sensor and object, producing dense flow without soft-body physics.

sections.heading: How does a rigid-body simulator calculate slip and twist?
sections.summary: Running on IsaacLab, TactileLab outputs low-dimensional contact forces as well as two high-dimensional modalities: contact depth images and simulated tactile flow. Flow is computed by projecting minute displacements of surface points within the contact patch onto the camera plane at near-zero extra cost.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B TactileLab Overview and Multimodal Touch
TactileLab is built on NVIDIA IsaacLab and fully supports GPU-parallel simulation. The simulated tactile modalities fall into two categories:
- Low-dimensional contact information $\mathbf{c}_t$: contact forces, contact positions, and shear vectors. These are used primarily as privileged information or for analysis.
- High-dimensional contact observations: a contact depth image $\mathbf{D}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W}$ representing local normal penetration, and a simulated tactile flow field $\mathbf{F}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 2}$ capturing tangential displacement.

### III-C Computing Simulated Tactile Flow
How can tactile flow be derived purely from rigid-body simulation? The mechanism is straightforward.
First, pixels where contact depth $\mathbf{D}_t$ exceeds a threshold $\epsilon$ form a contact mask $C_t$. For each pixel in this mask, the simulator identifies the 3D surface point $\mathbf{x}_t$ of the object penetrating the sensor surface. Over the time step $t+\Delta t$, relative rigid-body motion moves this point to $\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}$. Projecting both points onto the internal virtual camera via projection function $\Pi$ yields the pixel displacement $\Delta \mathbf{p} = \Pi(\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}) - \Pi(\mathbf{x}_t)$. Background pixels outside the contact patch are set to zero.

Rather than simulating the physical deformation of rubber, the method geometrically tracks where penetrating object surface points move on the camera plane. Contact depth reveals where and how deeply contact occurs, while tactile flow indicates which way the surface is sliding. Together, they capture shear-relevant dynamics cleanly and efficiently.

sections.heading: PETS-Net: Fusing long proprioceptive history with rich tactile images
sections.summary: RL policy training uses a two-stage Teacher-Student knowledge distillation setup. The student uses PETS-Net, an adaptation module that pairs positional encodings with spatio-temporal networks to handle rapid contact transitions.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Two-Stage Multimodal Learning Framework
Policy learning follows an established Teacher-Student paradigm:
- Stage 1 (Teacher Policy): An encoder $E_\psi$ compresses privileged exogenous variables $\mathbf{e}_t$ (object mass, friction, disturbance torques, ground-truth object poses) into a latent vector $\mathbf{z}_t$. A base policy $\pi_\theta$ is trained with RL (PPO) using $\mathbf{z}_t$ alongside a short proprioception/action history $\mathbf{o}^{\mathrm{base}}_t$.
- Stage 2 (Student Distillation): Keeping base policy $\pi_\theta$ frozen, an adaptation module is trained to predict $\mathbf{z}_t$ using only observations available on the real robot (joint angles, past actions, contact depth, and tactile flow). Training minimizes the mean squared error $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adapt}} = \|\mathbf{z}_t - \hat{\mathbf{z}}_t\|_2^2$.

### IV-C Architecture of PETS-Net (Positional-Encoding Temporal-Spatial Network)
Dexterous manipulation involves frequent finger make-and-break contacts, producing high-frequency state transitions. Standard neural networks often suffer from spectral bias, favoring low-frequency functions.
PETS-Net addresses this with three core components:
- Positional Encoding (PE) for Proprioceptive History: Sinusoidal and cosinusoidal frequency encodings across $K$ bands expand joint angles and action sequences into richer representations.
- Spatial Tactile Encoder: Contact depth and tactile flow pass through dedicated CNN backbones to extract local geometric and kinematic features.
- Temporal Encoder: Extracted tactile features and positionally encoded proprioceptive features are concatenated and processed by a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) over the past $l$ time steps.
This design effectively summarizes both spatial contact patterns and temporal transition contexts into a compact latent vector.

captions.F3: (a) Overall multimodal tactile learning pipeline for dexterous manipulation. Knowledge is distilled from a privileged Teacher into an observation-based Student under random external disturbances. (b) PETS-Net architecture, integrating positional encodings on proprioception with CNN-based spatial tactile encoding via a TCN temporal encoder.

sections.heading: TacFlowNet: Mapping real tactile streams to simulated tactile flow
sections.summary: The authors introduce TacFlowNet, which predicts pixel-aligned simulated tactile flow directly from two consecutive real tactile frames. Combined with static contact depth estimation, it feeds real-world camera inputs directly into simulation-trained policies.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B Real-to-Sim Tactile Flow Translation
To deploy simulation-trained policies on physical hardware, real tactile camera streams must be mapped into the simulator's input representation. While prior real-to-sim methods infer normal contact depth from single images, the key contribution here is predicting dynamic tactile flow from consecutive real images.

TacFlowNet uses a pix2pix-style generator $G$ taking channel-concatenated consecutive tactile frames $\mathbf{I}_t, \mathbf{I}_{t+\Delta t}$ to predict a 2-channel flow field $\hat{\mathbf{F}}$ matching the simulator's coordinates. Training uses a hybrid loss combining an adversarial loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adv}}$ and a masked L1 loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}}$ computed strictly inside the contact mask $\mathbf{C}_i$.

Crucially, TacFlowNet does not output optical flow of the real camera image. Instead, it translates visual deformation patterns directly into the simulator's defined physical relative motion field. This allows the system to extract shear flow from subtle shading variations and elastomer textures, even on markerless sensor surfaces.

captions.F4: Architecture of Real-to-Sim-TacFlowNet. The generator takes two consecutive real tactile frames and outputs a simulated tactile flow field, trained with a masked L1 loss inside the contact region alongside an adversarial loss.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: Data collection and two contact-rich benchmarks
sections.summary: Paired real and simulated data were gathered across pressing, sliding, tilting, and twisting motions. The framework was evaluated on dual-arm object-following (where shear is critical) and 16-DoF in-hand object rotation under continuous random disturbances.
sections.details:
### VI-A Tactile Data Collection Protocol for Real-to-Sim
To train TacFlowNet, an automated protocol sampled identical 6D contact poses $\boldsymbol{\xi}_i = (x, y, z, \alpha, \beta, \psi)$ and relative motions $\Delta \boldsymbol{\xi}_i$ in both the real world and simulation. On hardware, a robot arm executed prescribed trajectories against an indenter, recording initial and final image pairs. The exact same geometry and motion were mirrored in simulation to generate ground-truth contact depth and tactile flow. The dataset covers canonical contact dynamics: pressing, sliding, tilting, and twisting.

### VI-B Dual-Arm Object-Following Task
A follower arm must maintain contact at a target relative pose while a leader arm moves an object along unknown 6-DoF trajectories. Lateral displacement or rotation induces strong shear forces; depth images alone respond sluggishly, making tactile flow essential for stable tracking.

### VI-C In-Hand Manipulation Task
Using 16-DoF Allegro and LEAP hands, the goal is continuous object rotation around a target axis purely with fingertips (without palm support). To push robustness, hand orientation (gravity direction) was randomly varied, while continuous, unknown random 3D forces and torques were injected into the object. Preventing drops demands precise slip detection and coordinated finger gaiting.

sections.heading: Results: The impact of tactile flow, PETS-Net, and real-world execution
sections.summary: Simulations showed that tactile flow dramatically improved convergence, final reward, and drop rates, leading to emergent finger-walking (pinch-gaiting). On hardware, the policy successfully rotated completely unseen cubes and fruits without dropping them.
sections.details:
### VII-A Tactile Modality Ablations
Comparing observation inputs in in-hand manipulation revealed stark differences:
- Policies using high-dimensional inputs (depth and flow) substantially outperformed proprioception-only (HORA-like baseline) and low-dimensional contact baselines (AnyRotate-like baseline) in both learning speed and final performance.
- When evaluated individually, tactile flow consistently outperformed depth. Tangential motion dominates rotational control compared to normal penetration. Combining both modalities achieved the fastest training and lowest simulation drop rates (11.76% on in-distribution objects, 18.69% on out-of-distribution objects).
- With high-dimensional touch, policy performance saturated with history lengths of just 5 to 10 steps. Because the tactile observations are highly informative, the policy requires fewer past frames to infer dynamic state.
- Tactile-flow policies exhibited emergent "pinch-gaiting": two opposing fingers firmly grasped the object while other fingers cyclically engaged and disengaged to deliver rotational torque.

### VII-B PETS-Net Ablations
Validating the adaptation module showed that:
- Positional encoding (PE) noticeably accelerated learning over raw inputs. A frequency band count of $K=2$ proved optimal; larger values increased dimensionality and made optimization harder.
- Comparing TCN, GRU, LSTM, and Transformer for temporal integration, TCN achieved the highest reward with minimal memory usage. Transformers struggled to match this performance and consumed excessive VRAM.

### VII-C Real-to-Sim Accuracy Across Heterogeneous Sensors
Experiments evaluated marker-based sensors (GelSight Mini with markers, TacTip) and markerless variants (markerless GelSight Mini, 9DTact). For markerless GelSight Mini, direct regression from real images yielded a translational velocity MAE of $1.79\,\mathrm{mm/s}$, whereas passing through TacFlowNet cut the error to $0.34\,\mathrm{mm/s}$ (with $R^2$ jumping from -0.02 to 0.98). As long as contact deformation produces perceptible visual changes, TacFlowNet reliably maps real images to simulated tactile flow.

### VII-D Real-World Deployments
- In dual-arm tracking, the policy tracked rigid cubes as well as completely unseen soft balls and an irregular brain-shaped squishy toy, keeping position errors under 6.5 mm and orientation errors below 0.06 rad.
- In LEAP Hand in-hand rotation, 10 unseen everyday objects (cylinders, spheres, and cubes) were evaluated. Despite training exclusively on capsule shapes in simulation, the proposed approach (depth + flow) rotated all objects—including sharp-edged cubes—for 30 seconds without drops, averaging 1.95 rotations. The low-dimensional baseline (AnyRotate) failed at edges and corners, managing only 0.28 rotations. This highlights how high-dimensional tactile flow enables robust adaptation to discontinuous contact transitions.

captions.F5: Ablation over modalities and history lengths for in-hand manipulation. Adding tactile flow yields a sharp increase in reward, while performance reaches near-optimal levels with as few as 5–10 history steps.
captions.F7: Emergent "pinch-gaiting" enabled by high-dimensional depth and flow. Flow patterns reveal how the thumb and opposing fingers cyclically engage, transfer load, and release to sustain smooth rotation.

sections.heading: Tactile flow as a paradigm shift and open directions
sections.summary: In multi-contact, time-varying dexterous manipulation, low-dimensional parameterizations fail; dense tactile flow is essential. Serving as a sensor-agnostic physical representation, it effectively decouples simulation policy learning from sensor hardware specifics.
sections.details:
### VIII-A & VIII-B Why Tactile Flow Proved Decisive
For simple arm tracking, hand-crafting low-dimensional variables (like contact points and shear vectors) into a PID loop can suffice. However, in multi-fingered dexterous manipulation, contact points shift constantly while disturbances and micro-slips occur continuously. Collapsing contact into a handful of scalar values leads to combinatoric failure and severe partial observability. Dense, temporally integrated tactile flow acts as a near-"sufficient statistic" for contact dynamics, restoring observability to the system.

### VIII-C A Sensor-Agnostic Common Intermediate Representation
A standout design choice of TactileLab is inserting contact depth and tactile flow as a shared physical intermediate layer between simulation and the real world. Simulators do not need to reproduce complex elastomer optical traits or lighting. As long as a sensor-specific translator like TacFlowNet is trained, the same RL policy can run seamlessly on TacTip, GelSight, or other vision-based tactile sensors.

### VIII-D Limitations and Future Work
The authors point out several open limitations:
- Sticking Contact Assumption: The current Real-to-Sim framework primarily assumes contact regions stick to the sensor surface during deformation, leaving sudden full-slip transitions incompletely modeled.
- Rigid Approximation Constraints: Because flow is estimated via rigid kinematics, discrepancies occur when contact involves complex 3D curved surfaces. The authors note that extracting tactile flow from soft-body physics could be explored if computational budgets allow.

takeaways: In contact-rich manipulation, tangential shear and slip dominate over normal depth; providing dense tactile flow dramatically boosts RL sample efficiency and policy robustness.
Fast shear simulation capable of supporting large-scale RL does not require heavy soft-body physics—it can be derived purely from rigid-body contact kinematics and geometry.
Using physically interpretable fields as an intermediate layer (Real Image -> Depth & Flow Fields -> RL Policy) enables seamless sim-to-real transfer across heterogeneous tactile sensors.
Rich, high-dimensional tactile feedback drastically reduces the required observation history length, enabling responsive closed-loop control.
limitations: The method assumes sticking contact where the elastomer deforms with the object, leaving the gap during sudden, violent dynamic slipping events unaddressed.
Because it relies on rigid kinematic approximations, generated flow fields can diverge when dealing with intricate surface curvatures or large nonlinear elastomer deformations.
For markerless sensors lacking visible surface texture, extracting accurate tangential flow from raw images remains challenging, revealing an inherent dependence on sensor hardware traits.
